text:
### Uttaramegha

"Of the women wearing a parting in their hair." The <term>Amara-kośa</term> <gloss>a standard Sanskrit lexicon</gloss> states: "A woman is a <term>sīmantinī</term> <gloss>one wearing a hair-parting</gloss> and a bride." "Brought by a friend." It is brought by a friend or through the agency of a friend. The word "friend" is used to remove any suspicion of deception <note>referring to the fear that the messenger might be an imposter or the message a fabrication</note>. "News of the beloved" is <term>kāntodanta</term> <gloss>tidings of the husband/lover</gloss>. The <term>Amara-kośa</term> notes: "News, information, story, and report are <term>udanta</term> <gloss>tidings</gloss>." It is slightly less than the reunion itself, meaning it provides joy just like the reunion.

Now he delivers the message—

"O long-lived one, for the sake of doing a favor to me and to yourself,
Speak thus to her, your companion, who resides in the hermitage of Ramagiri:
'Unperished, your husband who is separated from you asks of your well-being, O frail one,'
For this, indeed, is the first greeting of living beings susceptible to misfortune." <note>Verse 41</note>

"To her" means this. O long-lived one, the suffix <term>matup</term> <gloss>a grammatical suffix indicating possession</gloss> is used here in praise, meaning your life is worthy because you perform favors for others. "For the sake of doing a favor" means to fulfill yourself through helping others. Although the act of helping takes an object, the use of the genitive case <term>ātmanaḥ</term> <gloss>of the self</gloss> is not contradictory, as it implies a relationship, similar to the expression "helping someone." As <term>Bhāravi</term> <gloss>a classical Sanskrit poet</gloss> says: "That is wealth by which one helps others." Likewise, <term>Śrīharṣa</term> <gloss>a Sanskrit author</gloss> says: "To help the righteous, to see wealth, and to travel through the sky." Thus, the statement of the scholar <term>Nātha</term>—that in some places the accusative case is seen and therefore applies to all—is actually the statement of someone without a master <note>implying the commentary is unauthoritative</note>.

Speak thus to that beloved. What should you say? "O frail one, your companion, your husband, residing in the hermitages of the mountain Ramagiri <note>often identified with Citrakūṭa</note>, is unperished," meaning he is not dead. He gives the reason for his being alive: "Being separated, experiencing the suffering of separation, he asks after your well-being." The verb <term>pṛcch</term> <gloss>to ask</gloss> takes two objects. Indeed, for living beings who are prone to sudden misfortune, this question of well-being is the very first thing that must be asked. The suffix <term>ṇyat</term> <gloss>a grammatical marker</gloss> is used here in the sense of necessity.

"With a thin body, <unclear>touching</unclear> a thin body; with a body hot from intense fever, <unclear>touching</unclear> a hot body;
With eyes full of tears, <unclear>touching</unclear> eyes shedding tears; with longing, <unclear>touching</unclear> the longing one."

<summary>This page contains a Sanskrit commentary on verse 41 of the Uttaramegha, detailing the instructions given to the cloud messenger to assure the Yakṣa's wife of his survival and inquiring after her welfare.</summary>
